questions.q: What's the basic motion for adding any task or container to a control flow?
options: Open the Toolbox and drag the task or container onto the Control Flow design surface
Type its name into the Properties window
Right-click Solution Explorer and select Add New Task
Tasks are added automatically based on the connection managers in the package
questions.explain: Every task or container is added the same way: open the Toolbox and drag it onto the design surface of the Control Flow tab.

questions.q: What does the connector arrow between two tasks represent?
options: A precedence constraint — it defines the order tasks run in and the conditions for running the next one
A data flow path carrying rows between two tasks
A visual-only element with no effect on execution
A connection manager shared between the two tasks
questions.explain: The connector between two control flow items is a precedence constraint, specifying execution order and the conditions under which the next task runs.

questions.q: Why rename tasks instead of leaving the default names like 'Execute SQL Task 1'?
options: Descriptive, unique names make a package self-documenting, so you don't have to open every task to know what it does
SSIS packages fail to run if any task keeps its default name
Renaming is required before you can add a connection manager
It has no practical benefit — it's purely cosmetic
questions.explain: Clear, unique task names make the control flow readable at a glance, which matters enormously as packages grow more complex.

questions.q: What happens when you press F5 to run a package inside SSDT?
options: The package runs as a design-time test — tasks turn green on success, red on failure, with no server required
The project is automatically deployed to the SSISDB catalog
SSDT opens the SQL Server Agent job scheduler
Nothing visible happens until the package is deployed
questions.explain: Running a package inside SSDT with F5 is a design-time test run — you get immediate color-coded feedback per task, with no server or deployment involved.

questions.q: In a control flow with a container that holds a task inside it, what does that nesting represent?
options: The container groups that task's work, and containers can repeat that grouped work — the basis for loops in Chapter 2
It means the inner task belongs to a completely separate package
Nesting a task inside a container is purely a visual grouping with zero runtime effect
Only Data Flow Tasks can ever be placed inside a container
questions.explain: Containers group and can repeat the tasks inside them — the same mechanism Chapter 2's For Loop and Foreach Loop containers use.
